text:
The standard deviation and the standard error get mixed up all the time. Both measure a spread... just not of the same thing. Take two hundred customers' ages. Their standard deviation is the spread of the data: about ten and a half years. But their average came from one sample. Ask two hundred different people... and it moves. How far it moves is the standard error: the spread of the estimate, the width of its sampling distribution.

[curious] So how can you measure that, when you've only ever seen one average? Divide the standard deviation by the square root of the sample size. Ten point five eight, over the square root of two hundred, gives zero point seven five. The ages spread over decades. Their average wobbles by less than a year.

That's a bold claim from one sample, so let's check it. Here's a population with a spread of twenty-five. Draw fifty values, and average them. Then do it again... ten thousand times. The averages pile up, with a spread of three point five. From one sample, the shortcut said three point seven. Close, without repeating anything.

Now, what does that square root cost? When data spreads by twenty, a hundred people give a standard error of two. Halving it takes four hundred. Halving it again, sixteen hundred. A tenth of the error takes a HUNDRED times the data. Precision gets expensive, fast.

So why does this number matter so much? It's the ruler the rest of inference measures with. A hundred and twenty conversion times average eight point two seconds, with a standard error of zero point two two. Step about two standard errors either way, and you get seven point eight to eight point six. That's a confidence interval. And a test counts how many standard errors an estimate sits from the value it's testing. Next, we'll build that interval properly.
